title: Resolução No. 23.732, de 27 de fevereiro de 2024 (amendments to Res.-TSE No. 23.610/2019 on electoral propaganda: AI, deepfakes and internet-platform duties)
authors: Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (rapporteur: Minister Cármen Lúcia)
verification: Full text read at origin 2026-11-05 via reader (page returned HTTP 403 to standard fetch, full text retrieved through reader): confirmed resolution of 27 February 2024 signed by Minister Cármen Lúcia, inserting Arts. 9º-B/9º-C/9º-D/9º-E/9º-F/9º-G, 27-A and 33-B/33-C/33-D into Res. 23.610/2019.
relevance: The most detailed electoral-court rules anywhere on AI in election campaigning, issued by Brazil's Superior Electoral Court and applied in the 2024 municipal elections and the 2026 general elections. It imposes an explicit, conspicuous labelling duty on any synthetic audio, image or video in campaign material (Art. 9º-B), bans outright the use of deepfakes to favour or harm candidacies, sanctionable as abuse of political power up to cassation of the mandate (Art. 9º-C), and prohibits chatbots simulating conversation with real candidates. It also creates platform duties: anti-disinformation terms of use, notification and reporting channels, ad repositories searchable via API (Art. 27-A), joint liability for failure to remove, and even election-focused data-protection impact assessments for large campaigns (Art. 33-D). A labelling-plus-liability model built by an election court rather than a legislature, distinct from both the EU and US approaches.

title: Guidelines for providers of VLOPs and VLOSEs on the mitigation of systemic risks for electoral processes
authors: European Commission (Directorate-General for Communications Networks, Content and Technology)
verification: Official library page read at origin 2026-11-05: guidelines formally adopted by the Commission on 26 April 2024 after a public consultation of 8 February to 7 March 2024; framed as support for the Article 35 DSA obligation and cross-referenced to DSA Arts. 14, 15, 17, 24, 26, 27, 36, 37, 38, 39, 40, 42 and 48. Full guidelines document not read.
relevance: The Commission's first guidelines under the Digital Services Act on electoral systemic risks, issued ahead of the June 2024 European Parliament elections and applying to the EU's very large online platforms and search engines. They set out how providers should assess and mitigate risks to electoral processes, including strengthening risk assessments, tackling disinformation, labelling AI-generated content, protecting elections-related illegal content handling, and enhancing transparency of political advertising and recommender systems. The document shows how the EU channels election-integrity governance through platform self-assessment supervised by the Commission rather than through a dedicated elections regulator. Limitations: guidance is indicative rather than binding, and its practical effect depends on DSA enforcement decisions.

title: Election Commission of India advisory directing political parties, candidates and campaigners to label AI-generated and synthetic campaign content
authors: Election Commission of India (reported and analysed by IndiaAI, the MeitY knowledge portal)
verification: IndiaAI (Government of India portal) article read at origin 2026-11-05: describes the ECI directive on labelling synthetic content and its 2024 Lok Sabha election precursors; the ECI advisory text itself was not read, and updated October 2025 guidelines (labelling plus watermarking) are reported by Indian Express but not read.
relevance: The Election Commission of India - the constitutional body running the world's largest elections - directed political parties, candidates and campaigners to prominently label synthetic and AI-generated campaign material with notations such as 'AI-Generated', 'Digitally Enhanced' or 'Synthetic Content', and to include disclaimers in social-media promotion. It builds on advisories from the 2024 general election telling parties to avoid deepfakes and distorted AI content that would disturb a level playing field. The approach is purely administrative and party-facing, with no statutory penalties, illustrating how a large Global South election authority uses soft power rather than legislation to govern campaign AI. Useful counterpoint to Brazil's judicially enforceable rules and the EU's platform duties.

title: Altered Video of President Biden - Meta Oversight Board decision and recommendations on manipulated media policy
authors: Oversight Board for Meta (independent adjudication body)
verification: Decision page read at origin 2026-11-05: case fb-gw8by1y3 decided 5 February 2024; holdings, policy criticism and the three recommendations summarised above were read directly.
relevance: The landmark decision in which Meta's independent Oversight Board upheld leaving up a crudely edited ('cheap fake') video of President Biden, but declared Meta's Manipulated Media Network Policy 'incoherent' and unjustified: too narrow (video-only, AI-only, speech-only), with no clearly legitimate harm identified under ICCPR Article 19, and over-reliant on removal, which the Board warned can fuel accusations of cover-up and bias. It recommended a method-agnostic policy covering audio and depictions of people doing things they did not do, harms defined around voting rights, and labelling instead of removal absent another violation, with urgency given the 2024 global election year. A rare case of formal independent oversight reshaping a platform's AI-content governance rules; limitations are that it binds only Meta's content policy, not state law.

title: Surat Edaran Menteri Komunikasi dan Informatika Nomor 9 Tahun 2023 tentang Etika Kecerdasan Artifisial (Ministerial Circular No. 9 of 2023 on Artificial Intelligence Ethics)
authors: Ministry of Communication and Informatics of the Republic of Indonesia (Minister Budi Arie Setiadi)
institution: Ministry of Communication and Informatics (Kominfo/Komdigi), Indonesia
verification: Official JDIH Komdigi legal-database record read at origin 2026-11-05: stipulation and promulgation dates both 19-12-2023, signed by Menkominfo Budi Arie Setiadi; the record lists nine AI ethics values (inclusivity, humanity, security, accessibility, transparency, credibility and accountability, personal data protection, sustainable development, intellectual property) and status BERLAKU (in force). Circular text itself not read.
relevance: Indonesia's first national instrument on AI, issued as a non-binding ministerial circular days before the 2024 election year. It sets out nine ethics values - inclusivity, humanity, security, accessibility, transparency, credibility and accountability, personal data protection, sustainable development, and intellectual property - as a reference for business actors and electronic system providers developing or using AI, with control to be strengthened through funding, facilitation and supervision. Violations are channelled to existing law such as the Electronic Information and Transactions Law rather than AI-specific penalties. A representative case of soft-law first steps in Southeast Asia: fast to issue, low in coercive force, and a marker against which Indonesia's later PDP-law enforcement and AI policy can be measured.

title: Opinion 28/2024 on certain data protection aspects related to the processing of personal data in the context of AI models
authors: European Data Protection Board (adopted at the request of the Irish Data Protection Commission)
verification: EDPB press release read at origin 2026-11-05: Opinion adopted in Brussels on 18 December 2024; the three questions (anonymity, legitimate interest, consequences of unlawful processing in development) and key conclusions summarised were read directly. Full 35-page opinion PDF not read.
relevance: The EDPB's most consequential statement on how the GDPR applies to AI models, requested by the Irish DPC to promote harmonisation across EU regulators. It holds that models trained on personal data cannot be presumed anonymous (case-by-case assessment of memorisation and extraction risk); that legitimate interest can generally serve as the legal basis for developing and deploying AI models only through a strict three-step necessity-and-balancing test with mitigating measures; and that processing personal data unlawfully during development can taint the lawfulness of downstream deployment unless the model is duly anonymised. The opinion has become the reference point for GDPR-AI compliance debates and supervisory practice. Limitations: it is guidance, not law, and leaves hard questions to national DPAs' case-by-case analysis.

title: PIPC penalty surcharge and administrative fine on Meta Platforms for unlawful processing of sensitive personal data (KRW 21.6232 billion)
authors: Personal Information Protection Commission (Personal Information Protection Commission, Republic of Korea)
institution: Personal Information Protection Commission (PIPC), Republic of Korea
verification: PIPC official English notice read at origin 2026-11-05: resolution at the 18th plenary meeting on 4 November 2024, announced 5 November; combined penalty surcharge and fine of KRW 21.6232 billion; findings on sensitive-data profiling of about 980,000 users, improper refusal of access requests, and a small breach, plus correction orders.
relevance: Korea's privacy regulator sanctioned Meta with a record KRW 21.6 billion (about USD 15.6 million) for inferring and processing highly sensitive traits - religious and political views, same-sex marital status, interest in North Korea-related content - from about 980,000 Korean users' Facebook behaviour without the separate consent required for sensitive data under the Personal Information Protection Act, then sold those ad-targeting categories to around 4,000 advertisers. The commission also found unlawful refusal of access requests and inadequate authentication practices. One of the largest Asian enforcement actions against behavioural AI-style profiling, showing a rights-protective model running in parallel with Korea's promotion-first AI Framework Act. Meta reportedly appealed; compliance monitoring continues under the correction orders.

title: Medida Preventiva: ANPD determination suspending Meta's use of personal data for generative AI training in Brazil (Voto No. 11/2024/DIR-MW/CD; Despacho Decisório No. 20/2024/PR/ANPD)
authors: Autoridade Nacional de Proteção de Dados (ANPD), Conselho Diretor
verification: ANPD official news page read at origin 2026-11-05: preventive measure of 2 July 2024 with daily fine of R$ 50,000, grounds drawn from Voto No. 11/2024/DIR-MW/CD (inadequate legitimate-interest basis, obstacles to rights, children's data), links to the vote PDF and DOU publication. The 30 August 2024 lifting after Meta's adjustments is reported in secondary coverage but was not verified on this page.
relevance: Brazil's data protection authority used its new LGPD powers to suspend Meta's plan to train generative AI on the personal data of Brazilians (Facebook alone has about 102 million Brazilian users), finding that a 'legitimate interest' basis could not cover sensitive data, that users could not expect old posts to train AI that did not exist when posted, that opt-out obstacles were excessive, and that children's data lacked the required best-interest safeguards. The authority acted ex officio within days of the policy change, invoking grave and irreversible harm. Widely studied as the leading Global-South enforcement action on AI training data; secondary reports indicate the restriction was lifted in late August 2024 after Meta presented adjustments, which makes it equally a case study in the negotiation between regulators and platforms.

title: Kenya High Court determination on Worldcoin's biometric data collection (enforcement of the Data Protection Act, 2019)
authors: High Court of Kenya (R.E. Aburili J); scholarly analysis by the Centre for Intellectual Property and Information Technology Law (CIPIT), Strathmore University
institution: High Court of Kenya; CIPIT, Strathmore University (analysis)
verification: CIPIT (Strathmore University) analysis read at origin 2026-11-05: ruling of 5 May 2025 by R.E. Aburili J, holdings on consent, DPIA, cross-border transfer and registration, and the deletion order supervised by the Office of the Data Protection Commissioner. The judgment text itself was not read.
relevance: In May 2025 Kenya's High Court declared Worldcoin's collection of Kenyans' iris and facial scans unlawful under the Data Protection Act 2019 and the Constitution: consent bought with roughly KES 7,000 in cryptocurrency was not free, specific or informed ('luring poor Kenyans with cryptocurrency bypasses the essence of informed consent'); no data protection impact assessment was done for high-risk biometric processing; data moved to servers abroad without required safeguards; and local processors were unregistered. The court ordered permanent, supervised erasure of the biometric data and a halt to collection, building on the ODPC's 2023 determination against Worldcoin entities. The most consequential biometric-surveillance ruling from Africa, now a reference point for data sovereignty and consent standards in the Global South.

title: Toolkit for Responsible AI Innovation in Law Enforcement
authors: INTERPOL Innovation Centre and the United Nations Interregional Crime and Justice Research Institute (UNICRI), funded by the European Union
verification: INTERPOL Innovation AI Toolkit page read at origin 2026-11-05: published June 2023, developed by INTERPOL with UNICRI with EU funding, comprising seven resources plus a user guide and to be implemented through training, cooperative projects and the INTERPOL Responsible AI Lab (I-RAIL); a revised toolkit was announced 6 March 2024 per the Innovation page.
relevance: The first global governance toolkit for police adoption of AI, produced by INTERPOL and UNICRI to help law-enforcement agencies institutionalise responsible AI across development, procurement and use. Its seven resources include AI principles for policing, a technical reference book, risk-assessment questionnaires, an organisational roadmap and a workbook, covering use cases from emergency call centres to identifying exploited children while stressing human-rights and policing-principle safeguards, with particular attention to generative AI risks. It matters because most AI-governance debates regulate private-sector AI, while state coercion uses of AI (predictive policing, biometrics, triage) are governed mainly through voluntary frameworks like this one. Limitation: non-binding, and uptake varies widely across INTERPOL's 196 member countries.

title: Smart Justice? Making Sense of the Rise of Algorithm-Based Pre-trial Risk Assessment in Criminal Justice Through 'Legal Models'
authors: Georg Wenzelburger, Karen Yeung, Kathrin Hartmann
institution: Digital Society (Springer), vol. 4, no. 2; Saarland University and University of Birmingham
verification: OpenAlex record for DOI 10.1007/s44206-025-00194-7 read 2026-11-05 (title, authors, affiliations, publication date 11 June 2025, open-access status and abstract); the Springer article page itself was unreachable through automated fetch (cookie redirect).
relevance: A legal-theoretical analysis of the wave of US 'smart-on-crime' reforms that put algorithmic pre-trial risk assessment tools into bail decisions, co-authored by Karen Yeung, one of the leading scholars of algorithmic regulation. The authors interpret these reforms through three classic models of criminal justice - retributive, actuarial and preventive justice - and empirically find a shift away from censure and retribution toward crime prevention as the operative rationale. The paper shows that legal theory can clarify, but only partially capture, the values at stake when risk scores enter courtroom discretion. A useful bridge between the technical risk-assessment literature and debates on judicial discretion and legitimacy; its limitation is that the models predate algorithmic tools and the analysis is interpretive rather than causal.

title: Moffatt v. Air Canada, 2024 BCCRT 149 (tribunal liability for AI chatbot misinformation)
authors: British Columbia Civil Resolution Tribunal (Member Christopher C. Rivers)
institution: Civil Resolution Tribunal of British Columbia, Canada
access: open page (decision; automated fetch blocked, holdings verified via detailed legal analysis)
verification: CanLII decision page returned HTTP 403 to automated fetch on 2026-11-05; holdings verified against the ABA Business Law Today analysis (read 2026-11-05) and corroborating coverage (BBC, McCarthy Tétrault) from search results.
relevance: The first widely cited ruling holding a company liable for what its customer-facing AI chatbot says. Air Canada's website chatbot wrongly told Jake Moffatt he could book a full-fare ticket and claim a bereavement-fare refund afterwards; the tribunal found negligent misrepresentation, rejected the airline's argument that the chatbot was a 'separate legal entity' responsible for itself, and held that Air Canada 'bears responsibility for all the information on its website' whether static or chatbot-generated, awarding roughly CAD 812 including fees and interest. It establishes a simple consumer-protection baseline for conversational AI: firms own their bots' statements. Limitations: a tribunal decision with no formal precedent value outside British Columbia's CRT, and damages were trivial; its importance is doctrinal and symbolic.

title: SB 53 - Transparency in Frontier Artificial Intelligence Act (TFAIA), signed by Governor Newsom
authors: Senator Scott Wiener (author); signed by Governor Gavin Newsom
institution: California State Legislature; Office of the Governor of California
verification: Governor's press release read at origin 2026-11-05: signed 29 September 2025, authored by Sen. Wiener, requiring published safety frameworks, a critical-safety-incident reporting mechanism to the Office of Emergency Services, whistleblower protections with civil penalties enforceable by the Attorney General, and CalCompute. The 15-day reporting deadline and 1 January 2026 effective date appear in legal analyses (IAPP, Jones Day, METR) but not on this page.
relevance: California's SB 53 is the first binding statute anywhere to impose transparency and incident-reporting duties directly on frontier AI developers: covered companies must publish safety frameworks tied to recognised standards, report critical safety incidents to Cal OES (statutory summaries describe a 15-day deadline), and protect employees who disclose significant health and safety risks, with civil penalties enforceable by the Attorney General. It also launches CalCompute, a public computing consortium, tying safety governance to public compute capacity. Enacted one year after the SB 1047 veto, it represents the narrower, transparency-first model of frontier-AI regulation that survived politically. Coverage is limited to the largest developers, and effectiveness depends on what the published frameworks actually contain.

title: Veto message for SB 1047, Safe and Secure Innovation for Frontier Artificial Intelligence Models Act
authors: Governor Gavin Newsom
institution: Office of the Governor of California
verification: Full veto message read 2026-11-05 (PDF downloaded from gov.ca.gov and text extracted): 'I am returning Senate Bill 1047 without my signature', dated 29 September 2024, with the reasoning summarised below quoted verbatim in the text.
relevance: The primary document in the defining US fight over frontier-AI legislation: Governor Newsom's veto of SB 1047, which would have required safety protocols and a Board of Frontier Models for the largest model developers. The message accepts the need for action ('we cannot afford to wait for a major catastrophe') but objects that the bill's compute-cost threshold 'establishes a regulatory framework that could give the public a false sense of security' and 'applies stringent standards to even the most basic functions', preferring risk-based, empirically informed regulation and pointing to his signed sectoral bills and the state's critical-infrastructure risk analyses. Essential primary evidence for why liability-first model regulation failed in the US while transparency-first (SB 53) survived.

title: SB 24-205 - Consumer Protections for Artificial Intelligence (Colorado AI Act)
authors: Senator Robert Rodriguez (prime sponsor); Representatives Brianna Titone and Manny Rutinel; signed by Governor Jared Polis
verification: Official bill page read at origin 2026-11-05: introduced in the Senate April 2024, passed third readings 3 and 8 May 2024, signed 17 May 2024, status 'Became Law'; key duties (reasonable care against algorithmic discrimination, rebuttable presumptions, AG notification within 90 days, consumer AI disclosure) read from the page's summary.
relevance: The first comprehensive US state statute regulating high-risk AI across sectors: signed 17 May 2024 and, as enacted, effective 1 February 2026, it imposes on developers and deployers of high-risk AI systems a duty of reasonable care to protect consumers from algorithmic discrimination, backed by rebuttable presumptions tied to impact assessments, risk-management programmes, consumer notices, appeal rights with human review where feasible, and 90-day notification of discovered discrimination to the Attorney General, who holds exclusive enforcement authority through the consumer-protection law. It also requires disclosure when consumers interact with AI. Colorado became the template (and battleground) for state AI legislation, with later legislative sessions revisiting its timeline - a caution that algorithmic-discrimination duties remain politically contested.

title: Bill C-27, Digital Charter Implementation Act, 2022 (including the Artificial Intelligence and Data Act, AIDA) - LEGISinfo legislative record
authors: Parliament of Canada (House government bill sponsored by Minister of Innovation, Science and Industry François-Philippe Champagne)
verification: LEGISinfo page read at origin 2026-11-05: first reading 16 June 2022; second reading and referral to the Standing Committee on Industry and Technology (INDU) on 24 April 2023 (Votes 300-301); committee study September 2023 to 26 September 2024; report stage 'Not reached'; session ended 6 January 2025 with the bill at committee - i.e., lapsed on prorogation.
relevance: The official record of Canada's attempt to become an early AI regulator: Bill C-27 would have enacted, alongside privacy reform, the Artificial Intelligence and Data Act - a Minister-and-Commissioner model regulating 'high-impact' AI systems with a three-track penalty regime, developed through AIDA's distinctive iterative companion-document process. After dozens of INDU committee hearings and heavy criticism about vagueness and insufficient consultation, the bill died on prorogation on 6 January 2025 and has not been reintroduced, leaving Canada with no general AI statute. A canonical case study in how a middle power's AI legislation failed on process and legitimacy grounds, and in the gap between strategy documents and statutory capacity.

title: Measures for Labeling of AI-Generated Synthetic Content (人工智能生成合成内容标识办法)
authors: Cyberspace Administration of China, Ministry of Industry and Information Technology, Ministry of Public Security, National Radio and Television Administration (State Information Office Tongzi [2025] No. 2); English translation by China Law Translate
institution: Cyberspace Administration of China (with three other departments)
access: open page (unofficial English translation of the final measures)
verification: China Law Translate translation read at origin 2026-11-05: promulgated 7 March 2025, effective 1 September 2025 (Art. 14); provisions on explicit and implicit labels (Arts. 4-5), platform verification and user-declaration duties (Arts. 6, 10), filing and safety-assessment integration (Art. 12) were read directly. Official Chinese text and the accompanying mandatory national standard were not read.
relevance: China's horizontal labelling regime for AI-generated content, effective 1 September 2025 and tied to a mandatory national standard: providers of text, image, audio, video and virtual-scene generators must apply conspicuous explicit labels and machine-readable implicit metadata (provider identity plus content reference number); distribution platforms must verify metadata, alert users to possible AI content and offer user labelling tools; app stores check compliance; users must declare AI content, and malicious removal or forgery of labels is prohibited. Label materials must be submitted during algorithm filing and safety assessments, embedding the rules in China's existing registration system for recommendation algorithms, deep synthesis and generative AI services. The most complete state-mandated provenance regime anywhere, though enforced within a system without independent oversight.

title: Digital Omnibus on AI - Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 of 8 July 2026 amending Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act)
authors: European Parliament and Council (originating from the European Commission's Digital Omnibus proposal of 19 November 2025)
verification: AI Act Explorer (Future of Life Institute) page read at origin 2026-11-05: hosts the final text of Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, adopted 8 July 2026 and in force 27 July 2026; postponements (high-risk obligations to 2 December 2027 for Annex III and 2 August 2028 for Annex I), new Article 5 bans, Article 4a, the EU-level sandbox and expanded AI Office powers (Arts. 75a-75d) were read from that page. The 19 November 2025 proposal date is per EPRS and law-firm reporting from search results.
relevance: The first substantive amendment of the EU AI Act: the omnibus, proposed in November 2025 amid industry and transatlantic pressure and adopted on 8 July 2026, delays high-risk obligations by roughly 18 months (to 2 December 2027 for Annex III systems and 2 August 2028 for product-embedded high-risk AI), adds new bans on AI generating non-consensual intimate imagery and CSAM, allows exceptional processing of special-category data for bias detection and correction (Art. 4a), creates an EU-level GPAI sandbox, gives the AI Office inspection, commitment, fine and periodic-penalty powers (Arts. 75a-75d), and simplifies documentation and fines for SMEs and small mid-caps. It shows the EU recalibrating its flagship statute after adoption - essential for anyone tracking whether the AI Act's risk architecture is settling or unravelling. In force 27 July 2026.

title: Artificial Intelligence (AI) Guidance for Judicial Office Holders
authors: Courts and Tribunals Judiciary, England and Wales (Judicial Office)
verification: Full guidance (8 pages, dated 31 October 2025) read 2026-11-05 via text extraction from the official judiciary.uk PDF; it updates and replaces the April 2025 version, which in turn refreshed the original guidance of 12 December 2023.
relevance: The senior judiciary of England and Wales sets the reference standard for how judges may and may not use generative AI: no confidential or private information in public chatbots; verification of everything AI-provided, since hallucinated citations 'are not infrequent'; personal judicial responsibility ('AI tools may assist, but they cannot replace direct judicial engagement with evidence'); awareness of bias; and new sections on spotting AI-drafted submissions from unrepresented litigants, deepfaked evidence and 'white text' hidden prompts. Legal research and legal analysis are listed as tasks 'not recommended'. First issued December 2023 and refreshed repeatedly, it is the most-cited judicial-AI guidance in the common-law world. Limits: it governs conduct, not case outcomes, and enforcement is through judicial leadership rather than sanction.

title: Large Legal Fictions: Profiling Legal Hallucinations in Large Language Models
authors: Matthew Dahl, Varun Magesh, Mirac Suzgun, Daniel E. Ho
institution: Journal of Legal Analysis (Oxford University Press), vol. 16, no. 1, pp. 64-93 (2024); Stanford RegLab
verification: arXiv abstract page read at origin 2026-11-05: confirms authorship, the Journal of Legal Analysis 16(1) 2024 publication, and headline findings (hallucination rates 58 percent with ChatGPT 4 to 88 percent with Llama 2 on specific verifiable questions about random federal court cases; typology of legal hallucinations; models do not always know when they hallucinate). Full paper not read.
relevance: The study that quantified the fake-citation crisis reshaping court rules and lawyer sanctions: asking models specific, verifiable questions about random federal court cases produced legal hallucinations in 58 percent (ChatGPT 4) to 88 percent (Llama 2) of responses, with a typology distinguishing fabricated rules from fabricated cases and evidence that models fail to correct users' false legal premises and 'do not always know' when they hallucinate. The authors warn against unsupervised LLM use in legal tasks, with the greatest risk for self-represented litigants. It supplied the empirical basis for the wave of judicial AI guidance (including the UK guidance) and special-master orders. Limitations: pre-reasoning-era models and static snapshots of rapidly improving systems.

title: NAIC Model Bulletin: Use of Artificial Intelligence Systems by Insurers
authors: National Association of Insurance Commissioners, Big Data and Artificial Intelligence (H) Working Group
institution: National Association of Insurance Commissioners (NAIC), United States
verification: Full bulletin text read 2026-11-05 via text extraction from the official NAIC PDF: adopted by the Innovation, Cybersecurity and Technology (H) Committee 1 December 2023 and by Executive (EX) Committee and Plenary 4 December 2023; Sections 1-4 (legislative authority, definitions, AIS Program guidance, examination considerations) read directly.
relevance: The model that carried AI governance into US insurance regulation: adopted 4 December 2023 and since taken up by a large majority of states, it expects every insurer to maintain a written AIS Program governing AI across the whole insurance lifecycle - product development, marketing, underwriting and pricing, claims and fraud detection - with board-level accountability, bias testing and validation of predictive models, model-drift monitoring, third-party vendor due diligence and audit rights, and detailed documentation that departments may demand in market-conduct examinations. It anchors AI decisions to existing unfair-trade-practice and unfair-discrimination law rather than new substantive AI rules. The clearest sectoral, exam-based alternative to the EU's horizontal ex ante model, and the reference point for actuarial and underwriting AI accountability.

title: Opinion on Artificial Intelligence Governance and Risk Management in the insurance sector
authors: European Insurance and Occupational Pensions Authority (EIOPA)
verification: EIOPA publication page read at origin 2026-11-05: Opinion published 6 August 2025, addressed to national competent authorities, following a risk-based and proportionate approach and a public consultation on the draft earlier in 2025 with an accompanying impact assessment. Full opinion PDF not read.
relevance: The EU insurance supervisor's framework for supervising AI use in insurance, issued as an Opinion to national competent authorities in August 2025. It clarifies how existing insurance-sector legislation applies to AI systems and sets supervisory expectations on a risk-based, proportionate basis - continuing EIOPA's line (from its 2021 AI governance principles) that current insurance AI use cases are not automatically high-risk under the EU AI Act. Together with the NAIC bulletin it shows financial regulators converging on governance-and-supervision models (board accountability, model risk management, proportionality) rather than ex ante product approval for actuarial and underwriting AI. Limitations: an Opinion binding no one directly, and its practical weight depends on national supervisors' uptake.
